title: 26  Building regional embeddings: a simple example
text:
26.1 Overview
The sits package allows building of customized embeddings of data cubes using self-supervised learning. Any regular data cube, including multi-year and multi-modal ones, can be used as input. It is also recommended, but not mandatory, that a classified data cube for the same region and timeframe is used as a basis for selecting a stratified training sample. Users can thus design regional foundational models designed for specific cases and thus produce embeddings that are arguably better align with their desired products. The embedding workflow takes satellite image time series, learns a compact representation with a deep-learning encoder, and then runs a standard classification pipeline on those embeddings instead of on the raw bands.

title: 26  Building regional embeddings: a simple example
text:
26.2 Processing pipeline

26.2.1 Selecting the area of interest
In this chapter, we will use a small data cube to demonstrate the capabilities of the embedding-related functions in sits. In practice, one could use bigger data cubes to conver large regions of interest.
In this case, we will take the state of Rondonia, Brazil as our area of interest. Rondônia covers 237,765 km² — roughly the size of the United Kingdom. Almost all of it lies within the Amazon biome; original forest cover was on the order of 208,000 km². Rondônia is the most transformed state in the Brazilian Amazon. As of 2026, native vegetation covers 60% of the state — the lowest proportion of any Amazon state — with roughly 7 million hectares (70,000 km²) of native vegetation lost since 1985.
Pasture expanded from 7% of the state’s territory in 1985 to 37% in 2024 — approximately 88,000 km². Across the Amazon as a whole, over 90% of deforested area had pasture as its first use, and Rondônia is the state that converted the most native vegetation to pasture in absolute terms. The herd stands at roughly 18.2 million head (IBGE, 2023) in a state of 1.8 million people. Soy reached 717,600 hectares in the 2025/26 season. Expansion follows the pattern of converting degraded pasture rather than clearing forest directly, typically in soy-maize double-cropping systems.
Rondônia is an unusually demanding test case, and a useful one. Within one state you have the full sequence of Amazonian land change, plus the specific classes that make satellite image time series necessary rather than optional: pasture in varying degrees of degradation, secondary forest of differing ages, single-cropped versus double-cropped fields, and pasture-to-cropland transitions that are invisible in a single-date image but obvious in an annual spectrotemporal trajectory.
In this example, we will create a data cube using images from the Brazil Data Cube (“BDC”). Since the BDC already provides regular data cubes, there is no need for regularization. When using ARD data from other providers (e.g., CDSE or MPC), users need to copy the data to a local repository and obtain a regular data cube. The code for creating the data cubes is shown below.


R
Python




# Extract the shapefile with the boundaries of the Rondonia state
rondonia_shp <- system.file("extdata/shapefiles/rondonia/rondonia.shp", package = "sitsdata")

# Read the shapefile as an sf object
rondonia_sf <- sf::st_read(rondonia_shp)

# Define a Sentinel-2 data cube covering Rondonia in the Brazil Data Cube service
# We take 2022 as our study year
rondonia_cube <- sits_cube(
    source = "BDC",
    collection = "SENTINEL-2-16D",
    roi = rondonia_sf,
    start_date = "2022-01-05",
    end_date   = "2022-12-23"
)




# Import GeoPandas
import geopandas as gpd

# Extract the shapefile with the boundaries of the Rondonia state
rondonia_shp = r_package_dir("extdata/shapefiles/rondonia/rondonia.shp", package = "sitsdata")

# Read the shapefile as a GeoDataFrame object
rondonia_sf = gpd.read_file(rondonia_shp)

# Define a Sentinel-2 data cube covering Rondonia in the Brazil Data Cube service
# We take 2022 as our study year
rondonia_cube = sits_cube(
    source = "BDC",
    collection = "SENTINEL-2-16D",
    roi = rondonia_sf,
    start_date = "2022-01-05",
    end_date   = "2022-12-23"
)





26.2.2 Obtaining samples for representation learning
We start by selecting a large set of samples from an area of interest. This area should be large enough so as to capture spatial variations of the different classes. Depending on the representation learning method, one can use unlabeled samples; this is the practice for MAE, Barlow Twins, VICReg and LeJEPA techniques. For the Supervised Barlow Twins and Supervised Contrastive Loss method, we need labelled samples.
The training data for self-supervised learning is a set of unlabeled samples, which can be drawn in two ways: (a) Select a random sample from the chosen data cube; (b) select a stratified sample based on a classified data cube that covers the same region as the original. Although a random selection is simpler, using a classified data cube is recommended, since it enables balancing the samples between the different classes. In the first case, we use sits_random_sampling() and specify the total number of samples for self-supervised learning, as shown in the example below. When a classified data cube is available as a base layer, one can use sits_stratified_sampling() to aim for a an SSL sample distribution which captures frequent and less frequent classes. We show an example later in the chapter.
For this example, we take 30,000 samples covering the area of interest. In actual practice, a larger set of samples is recommended. Note that the next lines may take a long time. For this reason, we provide a shortcut in what follows.


R
Python




# select a random set of locations to be samples
random_locations <- sits_random_sampling(
    cube = rondonia_cube,
    n_samples = 30000,
    multicores = 8,
    memsize = 24,
    progress = TRUE
)

# extract the time series 
samples <- sits_get_data(
    cube = rondonia_cube,
    samples = random_locations,
    multicores = 8,
    progress = TRUE
)




# select a random set of locations to be samples
random_locations = sits_random_sampling(
    cube = rondonia_cube,
    n_samples = 30000,
    multicores = 8,
    memsize = 24,
    progress = True
)

# extract the time series
samples = sits_get_data(
    cube = rondonia_cube,
    samples = random_locations,
    multicores = 8,
    progress = True
)




The resulting samples consist of 30,000 time series covering a one-year period. Because of the time required to obtain the samples, we provide a shortcut by pre-archiving the result in the sitsdata package.


R
Python




# Get the samples from Hugging Face
samples <- sits_from_hf(
  repo = "e-sensing/samples_book",
  file = "rondonia30k.parquet",
  type = "dataset"

# use only optical bands, not indexes
samples <- sits_select(
    samples,
    bands = c("B02", "B03", "B04", "B05", "B06", 
              "B07", "B08", "B11", "B12", "B8A")
)

26.2.3 Building the weights of the encoder
To build the encoder, we need to select a representation learning method. For this example, we will use the VICReg (Variance-Invariance-Covariance) regularization method. For a detailed description of VICReg, please see the previous chapter.
To create the encoder, we use sits_pre_train() which takes two parameters: samples, which are the unlabeled samples to be used by chosen method; and rl_method, the chosen representation learning method. The example uses sits_ssl_vicreg(), whose parameters are described above. The most relevant choices are embedding_dim (size of the embedding vector) and encoder_model (the deep learning model used to process the inputs). In this case, we use sits_tempcnn().


R
Python




vicreg_encoder <- sits_pre_train(
    samples = samples,
    rl_method = sits_ssl_vicreg(
        embedding_dim    = 64L,
        encoder_model    = sits_tempcnn()
    )
)




vicreg_encoder = sits_pre_train(
    samples = samples,
    rl_method = sits_ssl_vicreg(
        embedding_dim    = 64,
        encoder_model    = sits_tempcnn()
    )
)




After obtaining a vicreg_encoder, we use it to produce embeddings from a data cube. In this case, we use the same data cube from the Classification of raster data cubes chapter. Please refer to that chapter for a description of the data.

Python

# builds a cube based on existing files

    collection = "SENTINEL-2-L2A",

# select only the S2 bands

The next step is to produce embeddings from the data cube. The original data cube has 10 bands and 23 time steps, and the encoding reduces it to 64 dimensions using sits_encode. The main parameters are data (either samples or a regular data cube) and encoder(which is the vicreg_encoder we derived from the samples). Note that the bands and timelines of both data and encoder must match for the function to execute correctly. The other parameters are memsize (RAM available), multicores (number of cores allocated), gpu_memory (if a GPU is available) and batch_size, which is used only when working with a GPU.
After generating the embeddings cube, we plot some of its dimensions.

section: 26.3 Selecting the labelled data for classification
text:
26.3 Selecting the labelled data for classification
The next step is to select the data for classification. In this case, we will use a subset of the samples_deforestation_rondonia sample set, which consists of 6,007 samples for different land use and land cover classes in Rondonia. There are nine classes: Clear_Cut_Bare_Soil, Clear_Cut_Burned_Area, Mountainside_Forest, Forest, Riparian_Forest, Clear_Cut_Vegetation, Water, Wetland, and Seasonally_Flooded. Each time series contains values from Sentinel-2/2A bands B02, B03, B04, B05, B06, B07, B8A, B08, B11 and B12, from 2022-01-05 to 2022-12-23 in 16-day intervals.
This is the same data set used in the Classification of raster data cubes chapter. To test the hypothesis that embeddings needs small set fo samples for fine-tuning, we take only 20% of the original samples for classification.
After selecting the samples subset, we encode the samples to match the embeeding dimensions with the same encoder we used for the data cube


R
Python




# Get the samples from Hugging Face
samples_deforestation_rondonia <- sits_from_hf(
  repo = "e-sensing/samples_book",
  file = "samples_deforestation_rondonia.parquet",
  type = "dataset"
)
# selecting a subset of the original training data
samples_fine_tuning <- sits_sample(samples_deforestation_rondonia, frac = 0.2)

# transforming the samples to the embedding dimension
samples_embedding <- sits_encode(
    data = samples_fine_tuning,
    encoder = vicreg_encoder
)

# plot the embedded samples using t-SNE
plot(samples_embedding, mode = "tsne", perplexity = 30)




# Obtain the samples 
samples_deforestation_rondonia = sits_from_hf(
  repo = "e-sensing/samples_book",
  file = "samples_deforestation_rondonia.parquet",
  type = "dataset"
)

# random selection from tile
# selecting a subset of the original training data
samples_fine_tuning = sits_sample(samples_deforestation_rondonia, frac = 0.2)

# transforming the samples to the embedding dimension
samples_embedding = sits_encode(
    data = samples_fine_tuning,
    encoder = vicreg_encoder
)

# plot the embedded samples using t-SNE
plot(samples_embedding, mode = "tsne", perplexity = 30)








Figure 26.3: t-SNE plot of embedded samples.



t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) is a non-linear machine learning algorithm used for data visualization and dimensionality reduction. It transforms high-dimensional datasets with hundreds or thousands of features into a 2D or 3D map, making clusters and hidden patterns visible to the human eye[1]. t-SNE turns distances into probabilities, then matches them in 2-D. For each point, it converts distances to its neighbours into a probability distribution — nearby points get high probability, distant ones vanish. It then scatters the points randomly on a plane and moves them by gradient descent until the 2-D neighbour probabilities match the high-dimensional ones as closely as possible (minimizing KL divergence).
Alternative to visualisation using t-SNE include dimensions (plots the spread of each label in the embedding dimensions) and “PCA” (plot the first two principal components).


R
Python

samples_emb_wet = sits_select(samples_embedding, labels = "Wetland")

After obtaining the embedding cube and samples, the next step is to follow the established sits classification pipeline, as shown below. We use an multi-layer perceptron method (sits_mlp()) which is well-suited to work with embeddings.

)

plot(emb_map)

title: 26  Building regional embeddings: a simple example
text:
26.4 Summary
This chapter presented the functions that support the creation and use of Earth observation embeddings based on satellite image time series. The examples show how to select an initial set of samples for self-supervise learning, and how the resulting encoder is used to generate embeddings. The final part of the chapter shows how use EO embeddings for fine-tuning leading to land use and land cover classification.

text:
26.5 References




[1] 
L. van der Maaten and G. Hinton, “Visualizing Data using t-SNE,” Journal of Machine Learning Research, vol. 9, no. 86, pp. 2579–2605, 2008, [Online]. Available: http://jmlr.org/papers/v9/vandermaaten08a.html.

title: Vector data cubes
text:
A vector data cube is a multidimensional data structure designed to manage, analyze, and query vector-based geospatial data across spatial, temporal, and thematic dimensions. This model extends the well-established framework of raster data cubes—commonly used in remote sensing and Earth observation—to the domain of vector data, which comprises geometries such as points, lines, and polygons that represent discrete spatial features.
Vector data cubes are structured to encapsulate geospatial features that evolve over time and carry associated attributes. Each element of the cube corresponds to a spatiotemporal observation of a vector object, characterized by its geometry, timestamp, and a set of descriptive attributes. Formally, a vector data cube can be described as a collection of tuples:
\[
VC = \{ (g_i, t_j, a_{ij}) \}
\]
where \(g_i\) denotes the spatial geometry, \(t_j\) denotes a temporal instance, and \(a_{ij}\) is the vector of thematic attributes associated with geometry \(g_i\) at time \(t_j\).
The spatial dimension captures the geometric representation of real-world entities (e.g., land parcels, administrative units), while the temporal dimension allows for tracking changes over time, and the attribute dimensions store thematic variables of interest (e.g., land use class, vegetation type). Vector data cubes are particularly advantageous in contexts where object-based spatial representations are more appropriate than gridded data.
The sits package supports a restricted version of vector data cubes. In sits, the polygons that make up a vector data cube are computed using all temporal instances of a raster data cube. One of the key measures used to delineate polygons from a raster data cube is the local similarity between pixel values. In sits, these distances are computed from all bands and all dates of the data cube.
This representation is useful for classification of land parcels whose boundaries have been computed by segmentation algorithms or which are part of a land cadastre. The basic idea is that sits combines raster and vector information by classifying polygons based on time series defined by their interior pixels. The following chapters describe how to extract polygons for raster ime series based on segmentation methods such as the SNIC superpixels algorithm and how to use these polygons for object-based image classification.

title: 28  Object-based time series image analysis
text:
28.1 Introduction
Object-Based Image Analysis (OBIA) is an approach to remote sensing image analysis that partitions an image into closed segments which are then classified and analyzed [1]. For high-resolution images (1 meter or smaller), the aim of OBIA is to create objects that represent meaningful features in the real world, like buildings, roads, and water bodies. In the case of medium-resolution images (such as Sentinel-2 or Landsat), the segments represent regions of the image with similar spectral responses, which in general do not correspond directly to individual objects on the ground. These groups of pixels are called superpixels [2]. In both situations, the aim of OBIA is to obtain a spatial partition of the image into segments, each of which can then be assigned to a single class. When applicable, OBIA reduces processing time and produces labeled maps with greater spatial consistency.
The general sequence of the processes involved in OBIA in sits is:

Segmentation: The first step is to group together pixels that are similar based on a distance metric that considers the values of all bands in all time instances as well as their spatial location. We build a multitemporal attribute space where each time/band combination is taken as an independent dimension. Thus, distance metrics for segmentation in a data cube with 10 bands and 24 time steps use a 240-dimensional spectral space and a 2-dimensional Euclidean space. This distance includes both a spatial component (how far the pixel is from the center of the superpixel in terms of x and y coordinates) and a spectral component (how different the pixel’s spectral values are from the average values of the superpixel). The spectral distance is calculated using all the temporal instances of the bands. The result is a set of superpixels: clusters of spectrally similar, spatially close pixels that correspond to coherent object parts in the image.
Training set selection: Users should provide a training set, consisting of either labeled points or polygons. We suggest using QGIS to label some of the polygons produced by the segmentation algorithm. These labeled polygons can be used to produce a set of consistent labeled points, using sits_get_data(). See more at “Time series from data cubes”.
Model training: Using the training set produced in the previous step, users produce a classification model using sits_train(). See more at Machine learning for image time series.
Classification: The next step is to classify the image using the model produced in the previous step. This step uses sits_classify(), which performs a pixel-based classification to obtain a set of probabilities. The segments are not used in the classification. They are saved for the next two steps: smoothing and labeling. Pixel-based classification is much faster than polygon-based classification and the results are equivalent.
Smoothing: Smoothing for vector cubes uses a different definition of neighborhood than raster-based probability smoothing. When dealing with raster cubes, neighborhoods are defined based on rectangular windows (e.g., 9 x 9 size). When dealing with a vector cube, neighborhoods are defined by the segments. In this case, all pixels inside a segment are considered part of the same neighborhood. When estimating the spatial effects, the probabilities of all pixels in the segment are used to calculate the smoothed probability of each pixel.
Map labeling: Once the set of probabilities has been obtained for selected time series inside a segment, they can be used for labeling. To label the segments, sits takes the probabilities assigned to each pixel inside a segment and uses an aggregation function to calculate the estimated value of class probabilities for each segment. The aggregation functions available include mean, median, and majority. After the aggregation, sits selects the label of each segment based on the maximum aggregate value for the class probabilities. This step uses sits_label_classification(), as shown below.

title: 28  Object-based time series image analysis
text:
28.2 Image segmentation in sits
The first step of the OBIA procedure in sits is to select a data cube to be segmented and a function that performs the segmentation. For this purpose, sits provides a generic sits_segment() function, which allows users to select different algorithms. The sits_segment() function has the following parameters:


Parameter
Meaning



cube
a regular data cube.


seg_fn
function to apply the segmentation


roi
spatial region of interest in the cube


start_date
starting date for the space-time segmentation


end_date
final date for the space-time segmentation


memsize
memory available for processing


multicores
number of cores available for processing


output_dir
output directory for the resulting cube


version
version of the result


progress
show progress bar?



Currently, there are two segmentation functions available: (a) sits_snic, which implements the Simple Non-Iterative Clustering (SNIC) algorithm; (b) sits_slic, which implements an extended version of the Simple Linear Iterative Clustering (SLIC). Both are described below. We suggest using sits_snic since it is much faster than sits_slic and produces good results in general.

title: 28  Object-based time series image analysis
text:
28.3 Simple non-iterative clustering (SNIC)
SNIC (Simple Non-Iterative Clustering) is a segmentation algorithm designed to partition an image into compact, uniform regions (superpixels) efficiently [3]. It is an evolution of the SLIC (Simple Linear Iterative Clustering) algorithm, described below. While SLIC relies on an iterative k-means approach (which requires multiple passes over the pixels), SNIC achieves similar or better results in a single pass using a priority queue, making it significantly faster and non-iterative.
SNIC treats image segmentation as a region-growing problem starting from a regular grid of seed points. It uses a priority queue to determine which pixel to process next, ensuring that regions grow in the “cheapest” direction first.
The algorithm can be summarized as follows:

Initialization: After choosing the data cube which will be segmented, users define the seed points (centroids) to be used to grow the superpixels. They can also choose their relative placement. The seeds can be placed on a rectangular, diamond or hexagonal grid, or can be placed randomly. A final parameter is the compactness, which defines how regular the shapes of the resulting superpixels are.
Priority Queue: Each pixel is represented in an n-dimensional feature space, defined by all the time instances of its spectral bands and its 2-D spatial position (\(x, y\)). The algorithm then creates a priority queue. Initially, the 4-connected neighbors of each seed are added to the queue. The “priority” (or cost) is the distance from the pixel to the seed’s centroid in the n-dimensional space.
Region Growing Loop, with the following steps:


SNIC initializes a label map — which tracks which superpixel each pixel belongs to — along with a corresponding distance map.
While the priority queue is not empty, the algorithm extracts the pixel with the smallest distance (lowest cost) from the queue.
If the pixel has already been labeled, it is discarded; otherwise, it is assigned to the superpixel of the seed that generated this queue entry.
SNIC updates the centroid of that superpixel immediately after adding the new pixel. The new centroid is the average of all pixels currently in that superpixel.
Unlabeled neighbors of the newly added pixel are added to the priority queue. Their cost is calculated based on the current (updated) centroid of the superpixel.
Go to step (b) until the priority queue is empty.

title: 28  Object-based time series image analysis
text:
28.4 Simple linear iterative clustering algorithm (SLIC)
The Simple Linear Iterative Clustering (SLIC) algorithm [4] clusters pixels into nearly uniform superpixels. This algorithm has been adapted by Nowosad and Stepinski [2] to work with multispectral images. SLIC uses spectral similarity and proximity in the image space to segment the image into superpixels. Here’s a high-level view of the extended SLIC algorithm:

The algorithm starts by dividing the image into a grid, where each cell of the grid becomes a superpixel.
For each cell, the pixel in the center becomes the initial “cluster center” for that superpixel.
For each pixel, the algorithm calculates a distance to each of the nearby cluster centers, using the same distance metric as that of the SNIC algorithm.
Each pixel is assigned to the closest cluster. After all pixels have been assigned to clusters, the algorithm recalculates the cluster centers by averaging the spatial coordinates and spectral values of all pixels within each cluster.
Steps 3-4 are repeated for a set number of iterations, or until the cluster assignments stop changing.

The outcome of the SLIC algorithm is a set of superpixels which try to capture the boundaries of objects within the image.

title: 28  Object-based time series image analysis
section: 28.5 Example of SNIC-based segmentation and classification
text:
28.5 Example of SNIC-based segmentation and classification
The SNIC implementation in sits uses the snic R package. The parameters for the sits_snic() function are:






Parameter
Meaning



grid_seeding
spatial organization of initial grid seeds (one of rectangular, diamond, hexagonal, random).


spacing
distance (in number of pixels) between initial superpixels’ centers.


compactness
numerical value between 0 and 1 that controls superpixels’ density. Larger values cause clusters to be more compact.


padding
distance (in pixels) from the image borders within which no seeds are placed.

sits_view(cube_20LMR, red = "B11", green = "B8A", blue = "B02", 
          dates = "2022-07-16")
sits_view(segments_20LMR, add = TRUE)








Figure 28.3: Detail of segmentation of image in Amazonia



After obtaining the segments, the next step is to classify them. This is done by first training a classification model. This case study uses the training dataset samples_deforestation_rondonia, available in package sitsdata. This dataset consists of 6007 samples collected from Sentinel-2 images covering the state of Rondonia. There are nine classes: Clear_Cut_Bare_Soil, Clear_Cut_Burned_Area, Mountainside_Forest, Forest, Riparian_Forest, Clear_Cut_Vegetation, Water, Wetland, and Seasonally_Flooded. Each time series contains values from Sentinel-2A/2B bands B02, B03, B04, B05, B06, B07, B8A, B08, B11 and B12, from 2022-01-05 to 2022-12-23 in 16-day intervals. The samples are intended to detect deforestation events and have been used in earlier examples of the book. For the training, we select the same bands as those of the data cube.
To begin with, we retrieve the training data from Hugging Face.


R
Python




# get the samples for deforestation in Rondonia from Hugging Face
samples_deforestation_rondonia <- sits_from_hf(
  repo = "e-sensing/samples_book",
  file = "samples_deforestation_rondonia.parquet",
  type = "dataset"
)




# load data
samples_deforestation_rondonia = sits_from_hf(
  repo = "e-sensing/samples_book",
  file = "samples_deforestation_rondonia.parquet",
  type = "dataset"
)






R
Python




# Select bands
samples_deforestation <- sits_select(samples_deforestation_rondonia,
                                     bands = c("B02", "B8A", "B11"))

# Train TempCNN
tcnn_model <- sits_train(samples_deforestation, sits_tempcnn())




# Select bands
samples_deforestation = sits_select(samples_deforestation_rondonia,
                                     bands = ("B02", "B8A", "B11"))

# Train TempCNN
tcnn_model = sits_train(samples_deforestation, sits_tempcnn())




The segment classification procedure applies the model to every pixel inside each segment. Each pixel is then assigned a set of probability values, one for each class. The output of the procedure is a raster data cube containing a probability layer for each class. The parameters for the sits_classify() function for vector cubes are:






Parameter
Meaning



data
either a data cube or a set of time series.


ml_model
a trained model that uses one of the machine learning methods provided.


impute_fn
an imputation function used to interpolate NA values (default = impute_linear).


multicores
number of CPU cores that will be used for processing (default = 2).


memsize
RAM memory available for classification expressed in GB (default = 4).


gpu_memory
GPU memory available for classification, expressed in GB, if a GPU is available and a torch-based model is used (default = 4).


batch_size
size of batches used for processing (default = 1000 x gpu_memory).


roi
Region of interest where pixels will be classified: either an sf object, a shapefile, or a numeric vector in WGS 84 with named XY values (“xmin”, “xmax”, “ymin”, “ymax”) or named lat/long values (“lon_min”, “lat_min”, “lon_max”, “lat_max”).


exclusion_mask
Areas to be excluded from the classification process, defined by either an sf object or by a shapefile.


start_date
Start date for the classification process.


end_date
End date for the classification process.


output_dir
Directory where results will be stored.


version
For version control.


progress
Progress bar to track processing steps.



:: Parameters for sits_classify in case of vector cubes.
In what follows, we compute the probabilities for the classes and visualize them. Note that the probabilities are computed on a pixel-by-pixel basis. The segments are used only in the subsequent function (sits_smooth() and sits_label_classification()).


R
Python




# Classify the vector cube using tempcnn model
segments_20LMR_probs <- sits_classify(
    data = segments_20LMR,
    ml_model = tcnn_model,
    output_dir = tempdir_r,
    gpu_memory = 8,
    memsize = 18,
    multicores = 6,
    version = "tcnn"
)
# Plot the probabilities for label Forest
plot(segments_20LMR_probs, labels = "Forest")



Figure 28.4: Probabilities for class Forest.






# Classify the vector cube
segments_20LMR_probs = sits_classify(
    data = segments_20LMR,
    ml_model = tcnn_model,
    output_dir = tempdir_py,
    gpu_memory = 8,
    memsize = 18,
    multicores = 6,
    version = "tcnn"
)
# Plot the probabilities for label Forest
plot(segments_20LMR_probs, labels = "Forest")





Probabilities for class Forest.






Then we can compute the smoothed probability cube. In the case of vector cubes, sits_smooth() works differently than the function does for pixel-based raster cubes. In the pixel-based case, users define a neighborhood as a fixed-sized window (e.g., 7x7 or 9x9 pixels). For vector cubes, each segment defines a neighborhood boundary. Inside the segment, sits_smooth() uses the neigh_fraction parameter to define the pixels that will be used to compute the resulting values. The smoothing method and the parameters are the same as described in the chapter “Bayesian smoothing for classification post-processing”; the only difference is the neighborhood definition. The parameters are:






Parameter
Meaning



cube
Probability data cube to be smoothed;


neigh_fraction
Fraction of neighbors with high probabilities used in Bayesian inference (default = 0.5).


smoothness
Estimated variance of logit of conditional class probabilities (default = 20).


exclusion_mask
Areas to be excluded from the classification process, defined by either an sf object or by a shapefile.


multicores
number of CPU cores that will be used for processing (default = 2).


memsize
RAM memory available for classification expressed in GB (default = 4).


output_dir
Directory where results will be stored.


version
For version control.


progress
Progress bar to track processing steps.





R
Python




segments_20LMR_smooth <- sits_smooth(
    segments_20LMR_probs,
    output_dir = tempdir_r,
    neigh_fraction = 0.5,
    memsize = 18,
    multicores = 6,
    version = "tcnn"
)




segments_20LMR_smooth = sits_smooth(
    segments_20LMR_probs,
    output_dir = tempdir_py,
    memsize = 24,
    multicores = 6,
    version = "tcnn"
)




Finally, we can compute the most likely class for each of the segments. For vector cubes, there is one additional parameter: label_method, which is used to define how the probabilities inside a segment will be combined. The options are mean (default), median, or majority. Based on the chosen option, sits will compute the probability for each class inside a segment. Note that all pixels inside a segment will be assigned the same probability value for each class. After this step, the function labels the segment with the class with the highest combined probability.
The parameters used in sits_label_classification() in case of vector cubes are:






Parameter
Meaning



cube
Probability data cube to be labeled;


label_method
Aggregation function for probabilities inside each segment (default = mean).


multicores
number of CPU cores that will be used for processing (default = 2).


memsize
RAM memory available for classification expressed in GB (default = 4).


output_dir
Directory where results will be stored.


version
For version control.


progress
Progress bar to track processing steps.





R
Python




# Label the smoothed probability vectors
segments_20LMR_class <- sits_label_classification(
    cube = segments_20LMR_smooth,
    label_method = "mean",
    memsize = 24,
    multicores = 6,
    output_dir = tempdir_r,
    version = "tcnn"
)
# plot the classified segments
plot(segments_20LMR_class, legend_position = "inside")



Figure 28.5: Plot of OBIA classified image.






# Label the smoothed probability vectors
segments_20LMR_class = sits_label_classification(
    segments_20LMR_smooth,
    label_method = "mean",
    memsize = 24,
    multicores = 6,
    output_dir = tempdir_py,
    version = "tcnn"
)
# Plot the classified segments
plot(segments_20LMR_class, legend_position = "inside")





Plot of OBIA classified image.

OBIA analysis applied to image time series is a worthy and efficient technique for land classification, combining the desirable sharp object boundary properties required by land use and cover maps with the analytic power of image time series.

title: 29  Creating vector data cube from local files
text:
29.1 Introduction
In many situations, users may want to create vector data cubes from local files. The most common case is when the want to recover a vector file has been previously created. An alternative is when users want to join a vector data file to a raster data cube. Recall that sits uses a specific notion of vector data cubes, which are polygons that cover an entire period of time. One example are farm boundaries for agricultural statistics.
To be used for classification, vector cubes are associated to a raster cube. In this way, classification is done on a polygon-by-polygon basis. Given a polygon which matches part of a raster cube, sits uses pixels inside the polygon to obtain a set of time series that are used for classification, as shown in the example below.
In what follows, we illustrate the procedure of linking vector and raster file.

title: 29  Creating vector data cube from local files
text:
29.2 Retrieving an external vector file
In this example, we will use a vector file developed by the “Fields of the World” (FTW) project [1]. FTW is a community-driven, global initiative that uses artificial intelligence and satellite imagery to map every agricultural field on Earth. Its aims are to detect and outline agricultural field boundaries at scale using machine learning and deep learning. It provide high-resolution boundary data spanning hundreds of countries and territories, mapping billions of individual field polygons. For more details in the project, please visit the Fields of the World website.
The selected FTW subset covers an agricultural area in the State of Bahia in Brazil and corresponds to an area inside the S13W46 grid provide by FTW in their website, defined by the bounding box with limits (lat_min = -11.82, lat_max = -11.57, lon_min = -45.75, lon_max = -45.52). The FTW file contains closed polygons which are geometrically consistent. The data is available in the sitsdata package, as show below.


R
Python




# directory where FTW file is located
fow_dir <- system.file("/extdata/fields_of_the_world", package = "sitsdata")
list.files(fow_dir)

[1] "SENTINEL-2_FOW_015009_2024-01-01_2024-12-31_segments_v1.gpkg"





# FTW file is available in a local directory 
fow_dir = r_package_dir("extdata/Rondonia-20LMR/", package = "sitsdata")
# List FTW file
files = [p.name for p in Path(fow_dir).iterdir() if p.is_file()]
print(files)



[1] "SENTINEL-2_FOW_015009_2024-01-01_2024-12-31_segments_v1.gpkg"





The FTW file has been converted from the original format geoparquet to a geopackage format, which is used by sits. Its name has also been changed to conform to the expected sits file format for raster and vector processed files, namely c("X1", "X2", "tile", "start_date", "end_date", "band", "version"). In this case, the components of the file name are split using _, and the first two elements are ignored (although we have included SENTINEL and FOW for clarity). The band type is segments. Any geopackage polygon file that contains these required items can be imported and linked to a corresponding raster file, as shown below.
For further information, please see the section “Reading classified images as a local data cube in this book.

title: 29  Creating vector data cube from local files
text:
29.3 Retrieving a local data cube
In this example, we will use an embedding cube covering the same region as the FTW segments. This cube has been produced using the scripts described in the “Building regional embeddings”. The original data consists of a two-year LANDSAT-8 cube for the period 2023-01-01 to 2024-12-31 covering the Brazilian Cerrado biome in monnthly intervals. To build the embedding, we used the JeLEPA algorithm [Balestriero2025] which is implemented by the sits_ssl_lejepa() function.


R
Python




# Retrieve a local embedding cube built with LeJEPA encoder
# data directory
images_dir <- system.file("extdata/Bahia-LeJEPA", package = "sitsdata")

# local cube
lejepa_cube <- sits_cube(
    source = "BDC",
    collection = "LANDSAT-OLI-16D",
    data_dir = images_dir,
    parse_info = c("satellite", "sensor", "tile", "band", "date")
)
# plot an RGB combination of three dimensions of the embedding cube
plot(lejepa_cube, green = "EMB10", red = "EMB12", blue = "EMB13")



Figure 29.1: RGB composite image for the LeJEPA embedding cube.






# Retrieve a local cube based with MODIS data
# data directory
images_dir = r_package_dir("extdata/Bahia-LeJEPA", package = "sitsdata")

# local cube
lejepa_cube = sits_cube(
    source = "BDC",
    collection = "LANDSAT-OLI-16D",
    data_dir = images_dir,
    parse_info = c("satellite", "sensor", "tile", "band", "date")
)

# plot an RGB combination of three dimensions of the embedding cube
plot(lejepa_cube, green = "EMB10", red = "EMB12", blue = "EMB13")





RGB composite image for the LeJEPA embedding cube.

title: 29  Creating vector data cube from local files
section: 29.4 Building a vector data cube for raster and vector files
text:
29.4 Building a vector data cube for raster and vector files
We now produce a vector data cube by associating the FTW vector file with the raster data cube produced above. To do this, we use the sits_cube() function, with the following parameters:






Parameter
Meaning



source
original source from which the data has been downloaded.


collection
image collection in data source.


raster_cube
raster cube to be merged with vector data.


vector_dir
local directory where vector files are stored.


parse_info
parsing information for metadata retrieval on local file.


delim
delimiter for parsing local files (default = “_“).


multicores
number of workers for parallel processing (default = 2).


version
version of the vector file (default = “v1”).


progress
show a progress bar?





R
Python




# create a vector cube by merging a raster cube with a vector file with segments
vec_lejepa_cube <- sits_cube(
    source = "BDC",
    collection = "LANDSAT-OLI-16D",
    raster_cube = lejepa_cube,
    vector_dir = fow_dir,
    parse_info = c("X1", "X2", "tile", "start_date", "end_date", "band", "version")
)

# plot the segmented cube
plot(vec_lejepa_cube, 
     green = "EMB21", red = "EMB22", blue = "EMB23", 
     seg_color = "white", line_width = 0.6)



Figure 29.2: Vector data cube for a small area in the state of Bahia, Brazil.






# create a vector cube by merging a raster cube with a vector file with segments
vec_lejepa_cube = sits_cube(
    source = "BDC",
    collection = "LANDSAT-OLI-16D",
    raster_cube = lejepa_cube,
    vector_dir = fow_dir,
    parse_info = c("X1", "X2", "tile", "start_date", "end_date", "band", "version")
)

# plot the segmented cube
plot(vec_lejepa_cube, 
     green = "EMB21", red = "EMB22", blue = "EMB23", 
     seg_color = "white", line_width = 0.6)





Vector data cube for a small area in the state of Bahia, Brazil.

title: 29  Creating vector data cube from local files
text:
29.5 Training a classification model
After building a vector data cube, we can now classify it, following the guidelines of the previous chapter “Object-based time series image analysis. We start by building a machine learning model using the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) algorithm. To do so, we use a samples of a labelled training set developed by the sits team for LUCC classification in the Cerrado biome in Brazil. The data set is available in Hugging Face.


R
Python




# Download the labelled data set from Hugging Face 
samples_cerrado <- sits_from_hf(
  repo = "e-sensing/samples_cerrado",
  file = "labelled_samples_cerrado.parquet",
  type = "dataset"
)
# Use 10% of  samples
samples_cerrado_frac <- sits_sample(samples_cerrado, frac = 0.1)
# plot cube
summary(samples_cerrado_frac)

# A tibble: 11 × 3
   label          count    prop
   <chr>          <int>   <dbl>
 1 Annual_Crop     1768 0.161  
 2 Cerradao         492 0.0447 
 3 Cerrado         3923 0.357  
 4 Mangrove          69 0.00627
 5 Nat_NonVeg        12 0.00109
 6 Open_Cerrado    1174 0.107  
 7 Pasture         2450 0.223  
 8 Perennial_Crop   163 0.0148 
 9 Silviculture     543 0.0494 
10 Sugarcane        334 0.0304 
11 Water             72 0.00655





# Download the labelled data set from Hugging Face 
samples_cerrado = sits_from_hf(
  repo = "e-sensing/samples_cerrado",
  file = "labelled_samples_cerrado.parquet",
  type = "dataset"
)
# Use 10% of  samples
samples_cerrado_frac = sits_sample(samples_cerrado, frac = 0.1)
# plot cube
summary(samples_cerrado_frac)



# A tibble: 11 × 3
   label          count    prop
   <chr>          <int>   <dbl>
 1 Annual_Crop     1768 0.161  
 2 Cerradao         492 0.0447 
 3 Cerrado         3923 0.357  
 4 Mangrove          69 0.00627
 5 Nat_NonVeg        12 0.00109
 6 Open_Cerrado    1174 0.107  
 7 Pasture         2450 0.223  
 8 Perennial_Crop   163 0.0148 
 9 Silviculture     543 0.0494 
10 Sugarcane        334 0.0304 
11 Water             72 0.00655





These samples were obtained by extracting time series for Landsat data cube. As such their data contains values for the original Landsat bands. To be used to train embeddings, they have to be converted to the same dimensions as those of embeddings cube. To do so, we follow the procedure used in the “Building regional embeddings” chapter, which is to transform the samples using the same LeJEPA encoder that produced the embeddings cube. For details on how to generate such encoder, please refer to the above-mentioned chapter. For brevity’s sake, we will use a version of the encoder which is archived in the Hugging Face repository.
To transform the samples to the embedding space, we retrieve the LeJEPA encoder from Hugging Face and use it to encode the samples.


R
Python




# Download the encoder from Hugging Face 
lejepa_encoder <- sits_from_hf(
  repo = "e-sensing/encoders_cerrado", 
  file = "ssl_lejepa_tcnn_model_2017_2024.rds",
  type = "model"
)
# Encode the samples to transform them into the embedding space
samples_cerrado_enc <- sits_encode(
    data = samples_cerrado_frac, 
    encoder = lejepa_encoder)




# Download the encoder from Hugging Face 
lejepa_encoder = sits_from_hf(
  repo = "e-sensing/encoders_cerrado", 
  file = "ssl_lejepa_tcnn_model_2017_2024.rds",
  type = "model"
)
# Encode the samples to transform them into the embedding space
samples_cerrado_enc = sits_encode(
    data = samples_cerrado_frac, 
    encoder = lejepa_encoder)




After converting the samples to the embedding space, we build a classification model using the multi-layer perceptron algorithm (sits_mlp()).


R
Python




# train mlp model
mlp_model <- sits_train(
    samples = samples_cerrado_enc,
    ml_method = sits_mlp(
        layers = c(256, 256, 256)
    )
)
# plot the evolution 
plot(mlp_model)



Figure 29.3: Accuracy and loss functions of the MLP model.






# train mlp model
mlp_model = sits_train(
    samples = samples_cerrado_enc,
    ml_method = sits_mlp(
        layers = c(256, 256, 256)
    )
)
# plot the evolution 
plot(mlp_model)





Evolution of accuracy and loss functions of the multi-layer perceptron model.

title: 29  Creating vector data cube from local files
section: 29.6 Obtaining a classified map using a vector data cube
text:
29.6 Obtaining a classified map using a vector data cube
To classify the cube vector_lejepa_cube, we follow the procedure described in Chapter “Object-based time series image analysis”. The first step is a pixel-based classification using the trained model to the probabilities associated to each pixel for each class. The memsize, multicores and gpu_memory parameters should be set by users according to the capabilities of their machines.


R
Python




# classify the embeddings cube to obtain class probabilities
vec_lejepa_cube_probs <- sits_classify(
    data = vec_lejepa_cube,
    ml_model = mlp_model, 
    multicores = 4,
    memsize = 8, 
    gpu_memory = 8, 
    output_dir = tempdir_r
)
# plot the probabilities of label "Annual_Crop"
plot(vec_lejepa_cube_probs, labels = "Annual_Crop")



Figure 29.4: Probabilites for class “Annual Crop”






# classify the embeddings cube to obtain class probabilities
vec_lejepa_cube_probs = sits_classify(
    data = vector_lejepa_cube,
    ml_model = mlp_model, 
    roi = segments,
    multicores = 4,
    memsize = 8, 
    gpu_memory = 8, 
    output_dir = tempdir_py
)
# plot the probabilities of label "Annual_Crop"
plot(vec_lejepa_cube_probs, labels = "Annual_Crop")





Probabilites for class “Annual Crop”.






After obtaning the probabilities, the next step is smoothing them. Given that the input is a vector data cube, each segment defines a neighborhood boundary for sits_smooth(). See the reference in the previous chapter.


R
Python




# smoothen the probability cube
vec_lejepa_cube_bayes <- sits_smooth(
    cube = vec_lejepa_cube_probs,
    multicores = 4,
    memsize = 8, 
    gpu_memory = 8, 
    output_dir = tempdir_r
)
# plot the probabilities of label "Annual_Crop"
plot(vec_lejepa_cube_bayes, labels = "Annual_Crop")



Figure 29.5: Smoothed probabilites for class “Annual Crop”.






# smoothen the probability cube
vec_lejepa_cube_bayes = sits_smooth(
    cube = vec_lejepa_cube_probs,
    multicores = 4,
    memsize = 8, 
    gpu_memory = 8, 
    output_dir = tempdir_py
)
# plot the smoothed probabilities of label "Annual_Crop"
plot(vec_lejepa_cube_bayes, labels = "Annual_Crop")





Smoothed probabilites for class “Annual Crop”.






The final step is producing a labelled classification map, based on the smoothed probability cube. For vector data cubes, sits_label_classification() performs segment-based labeling: pixel-level probabilities are aggregated inside each segment using the method specified by the label_method parameter. Options are “mean” (default), “median”, or “majority”. All pixels within a segment receive the same class label in the output raster. The GPKG file with segments is updated to include a class column.


R
Python




# label the vector cube with smoothed probabilities
vec_lejepa_cube_class <- sits_label_classification(
    cube = vec_lejepa_cube_bayes,
    label_method = "mean",
    multicores = 4,
    memsize = 8, 
    output_dir = tempdir_r
)
# plot the labelled map
plot(vec_lejepa_cube_class)



Figure 29.6: Labelled map for agricultural area in the state of Bahia, Brasil.






# label the vector cube with smoothed probabilities
vec_lejepa_cube_class = sits_label_classification(
    cube = vec_lejepa_cube_bayes,
    label_method = "mean",
    multicores = 4,
    memsize = 8, 
    output_dir = tempdir_py
)
# plot the labelled map
plot(vector_lejepa_cube_class)





Labelled map for agricultural area in the state of Bahia, Brasil.

title: 29  Creating vector data cube from local files
text:
29.7 Summary
In this chapter, we show how mix a vector file with a raster data cube to build a vector data cube. The vector file must be in the geopackage format and its polygons are contained inside the extent of the raster data cube. Also, the vector file name needs to provide adequate metadata. This allows much flexibility to users to combine external polygon files to sits.




[1] 
H. Kerner et al., “Fields of The World: A Machine Learning Benchmark Dataset For Global Agricultural Field Boundary Segmentation,” 2025, doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2409.16252.

title: Advanced Topics
text: The next chapters contains technical details on sits and are intended mainly for developers. It is intended to support those that want to understand how the package works and also want to contribute to its development. It includes general principles of sits software development, describes how parallel processing works. It shows how to support new STAC-based cloud collections and how to include new methods for machine learning in sits. It discusses how to export data to other packages and provides a comparison between SITS and Google Earth Engine.

title: 30  Exporting data to other packages
text:
30.1 R formats
This section demonstrates how to export sits data to commonly used data structures in R, facilitating integration with other R packages.

30.1.1 Exporting time series data to sf
The sf package is the backbone of geospatial vector processing in R [1]. To export time series tibbles from sits to sf, the function sits_as_sf() creates an sf POINT object with the locations of each sample and includes the time_series column as a list. Each row in the sf object contains the time series associated to the sample.

# Export a sits tibble to sf
sf_obj <- sits_as_sf(samples_modis_ndvi)
# Display the sf object
sf_obj

Simple feature collection with 1218 features and 8 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -60.4875 ymin: -17.4373 xmax: -51.565 ymax: -9.3126
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
# A tibble: 1,218 × 9
   crs                  geometry longitude latitude start_date end_date

30.1.2 Exporting data cubes to stars
The stars R package handles spatiotemporal arrays. It provides a general framework for working with raster and vector data. Data cubes in sits can be converted to stars objects using sits_as_stars(). By default, the stars object will be loaded in memory. This can result in heavy memory usage. To produce a stars.proxy object, users have to select a single date, since stars does not allow proxy objects to be created with two dimensions.

# create a data cube from a local set of TIFF files
# this is a cube with 23 instances and one band ("NDVI")
data_dir <- system.file("extdata/raster/mod13q1", package = "sits")
cube <- sits_cube(
    source = "BDC",
    collection = "MOD13Q1-6.1",
    data_dir = data_dir
)
stars_object <- sits_as_stars(cube)
# plot the first date of the stars object
plot(stars_object[,,,,1])





30.1.3 Exporting data cubes to terra
The terra package in R is a high-performance framework for spatial raster and vector data analysis. It was developed as the successor to the older raster package, offering a faster, more memory-efficient, and flexible API for working with geographic data. To export data cubes to terra, sits uses sits_as_terra() function which takes information about files, bands and dates in a data cube to produce an object of class SpatRasterDataset in terra. A SpatRasterDataset is an object that holds a collection of sub-datasets, where each sub-dataset is a SpatRaster sharing the same spatial extent and coordinate reference system. In terms of correspondence with sits, each sub-dataset holds all the bands of the data cube for a single time step. Therefore, the SpatRasterDataset will hold as many sub-datasets as there are time steps in the cube.

# create a data cube from a local set of TIFF files
# this is a cube with 23 instances and three bands ("NDVI", "EVI", "CLOUD")
data_dir <- system.file("extdata/sinop", package = "sitsdata")
cube <- sits_cube(
    source = "BDC",
    collection = "MOD13Q1-6.1",
    data_dir = data_dir
)
terra_object <- sits_as_terra(cube)
# show the contents of the SpatRasterDataset object
terra_object
